analysis.one_liner: Raises the federal minimum wage to $20 an hour over several years and ends subminimum wages for tipped and disabled workers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on February 10, 2026 with 6 total Democratic supporters and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee, where no further action has been recorded.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would raise the federal minimum wage from $7.25 an hour to $10 immediately after enactment, then to $13, $16.50, and $20 in yearly steps, and after that keep raising it automatically with inflation or GDP growth, whichever is greater [S2]. It would also phase out the lower 'tipped' minimum wage over six years so tipped workers get the full minimum wage plus their tips, raise the subminimum wage allowed for some workers with disabilities over six years and then end it entirely, and raise the youth training wage [S2]. It was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee on the day it was introduced, and the committee has taken no recorded action since [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly tens of millions of Americans paid at or near the federal minimum wage, who would see their pay step up to as much as $20 an hour over three years, with automatic raises thereafter. Tipped workers (servers, bartenders, salon workers) would get the full minimum wage on top of their tips within six years. Workers with disabilities currently paid below minimum wage under special certificates would be raised to the full minimum wage within six years.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the federal minimum wage in yearly steps to $10, $13, $16.50, and $20 an hour, then indexes it annually to the greater of CPI inflation or GDP growth, with rounding up to the nearest five cents [S2].

Phases the tipped minimum wage up over six years and then requires tipped employees be paid the full section 6(a)(1) minimum wage, while guaranteeing employees the right to retain their tips and requiring employers to inform them of that right [S2].

Raises wages under the Section 14(c) special-certificate program for workers with disabilities in yearly steps to $20 an hour over six years, then the full minimum wage; bars any new special certificates from the date of enactment and sunsets the program entirely after the phase-in [S2].
Raises the subminimum wage for newly hired workers under 20 from $4.25 to $6.00, steps it up annually, and repeals the youth subminimum once it catches up to the full minimum wage [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that pay minimum wage, especially restaurants that rely on the tipped subminimum wage, other low-wage service and retail businesses, and the small set of employers that hold special certificates to pay workers with disabilities below minimum wage. Some of those costs would be passed to consumers through higher prices; some low-margin employers in low-wage areas could cut hours or jobs to absorb them.

drawbacks.text: The bill raises the federal wage floor by nearly three times ($7.25 to $20) in three years, and a jump of that size falls hardest on small businesses and on lower-wage regions where prevailing pay is well below the new floor, where employers may respond by cutting hours or positions rather than prices [S2].

The bill repeals the separate wage schedules for tipped employees, workers under 20, and disabled workers, ending exceptions that some employers and some disability-employment advocates argue help employers offer entry-level or supported work; the bill only requires transition assistance to employers and referrals to competitive-employment resources for affected workers, not guaranteed placements [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gains for minimum-wage, tipped, and disabled workers are large and direct, and the automatic indexation means Congress would not have to revisit the wage floor again. The cost falls on labor-intensive employers, some of it passed to consumers. The rapid phase-in is aggressive relative to past federal increases, and the phase-out of subminimum certificates for disabled workers will require real transitions to competitive employment; the bill provides assistance and referrals rather than a funded placement guarantee. On balance the benefit to working people substantially outweighs the adjustment costs, though the low-wage regions and small employers most exposed would feel it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Education and Workforce Committee, which has taken no recorded action on it since.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Norcross (D-NJ) introduced H.R. 7471 in the House on February 10, 2026 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce on the day of introduction, the only recorded action besides introduction [S4].
Five House Democrats cosponsored the bill, for a total of six supporters, all Democrats [S3].
No markup, committee vote, floor vote, or Senate action appears in the recorded action history [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved; the employers who would pay the higher wages remain unaffected because the bill has not advanced, while the workers it would help have gained nothing.

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the committee on February 10, 2026; no further action, markup, or vote has been recorded since [S4].

sides.party_line_note: All six supporters (the sponsor plus five cosponsors) are House Democrats, and the Republican-controlled House committee has taken no action on the bill.

industries.note: The bill phases out the tipped subminimum wage over six years, then requires full minimum wage on top of tips, directly raising labor costs for restaurants, bars, and salons that currently pay the $2.13 federal tipped wage. That cost is the pay increase tipped workers would receive.

industries.industry: Low-wage service and retail employers generally
industries.note: Tripling the federal minimum wage over three years raises payroll costs for any business paying near the current $7.25 floor, with the largest effect in low-wage regions. Workers in those jobs would gain the same amounts employers pay.

industries.industry: Employers holding Section 14(c) disability wage certificates
industries.note: The bill raises wages for their workers to the full minimum wage over six years and then sunsets the program that lets them pay below minimum wage. New certificates are banned immediately.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the House Education and Workforce Committee with no recorded action, six supporters, and no Republican cosponsors. Minimum wage increases have historically not advanced from committee in a Republican-controlled House, so the likely path is that the bill stays referred and expires at the end of this Congress without a markup or floor vote.
